extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, policymakers, and readers of political philosophy (late 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century political pamphlet arguing for preservation of established institutions (church, monarchy, property) and against revolutionary subversion; addresses the proper foundations and duties of civil society. It lays out normative principles for government, religion, law, and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: We know, and, what is better, we feel inwardly, that religion is the basis of civil society, and the source of all good, and of all comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke asserts that religion underpins moral order and social stability; it should not be discarded as a 'rust of superstition' and remains preferable to impiety for the vast majority. Religion supplies consolation, moral incentives, and the common sense that sustains institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an established national Church
rubrics_metrics.description: We cleave closely to them. We are resolved to keep an established church ... I speak of our Church Establishment, which is the first of our prejudices,--not a prejudice destitute of reason, but involving in it profound and extensive wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An established Church is presented as integral to the constitution and public life: consecrating the state, supplying moral exemplars among rulers, supporting education, and linking classes. The establishment should be preserved rather than abolished or left to precarious private contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not call in atheism or radical doctrines to reform institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall never be such fools as to call in an enemy to the substance of any system to remove its corruptions ... If our religious tenets should ever want a further elucidation, we shall not call on Atheism to explain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should not seek its remedy from fundamentally hostile philosophies; radical metaphysics and atheism are 'unhallowed fire' that cannot be used to restore or perfect religious or civil institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gradual amendment over subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the evils of inconstancy and versatility ... we have consecrated the state, that no man should approach to look into its defects or corruptions but with due caution; that he should never dream of beginning its reformation by its subversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the state's faults 'as to the wounds of a father, with pious awe and trembling solicitude.' Radical breakage of institutions risks destroying continuity, education, law, and civilization; reform must respect inherited structure and be cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecrate public office by religious sanction to ensure virtuous governance
rubrics_metrics.description: This consecration is made, that all who administer in the government of men ... should have high and worthy notions of their function and destination; that their hope should be full of immortality ... and to a permanent fame and glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious consecration of state functions elevates office-holders beyond transient rewards and curbs corruption; it instills a sense of trust and accountability to a higher power, improving the moral quality of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion connected to the state fosters civic awe and restraints on popular licence
rubrics_metrics.description: The consecration of the state by a state religious establishment is necessary also to operate with a wholesome awe upon free citizens; because, in order to secure their freedom, they must enjoy some determinate portion of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that linking religion and state teaches citizens humility regarding power and deters the 'shameless' excesses of an absolute or unrestrained democracy; it prevents popular will from becoming the sole standard of right and wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve continuity of law, jurisprudence, and education
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of jurisprudence ... is the collected reason of ages ... Personal self-sufficiency and arrogance ... would usurp the tribunal. Of course no certain laws ... would keep the actions of men in a certain course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable, accumulated legal wisdom and steady institutions are necessary for education, arts, and manufacture; continual alteration of standards leads to barbarism and the breakdown of social learning and honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the state as an intergenerational partnership, not a temporary contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is, indeed, a contract. ... It is a partnership in all science, a partnership in all art, a partnership in every virtue and in all perfection. ... it becomes a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are dead, and those who are to be born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public institutions and constitutions are cumulative undertakings across generations; this moral and temporal continuity forbids whimsical dissolution or radical remaking for temporary advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property and inheritance against confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commons of Great Britain, in the national emergencies, will never seek their resource from the confiscation of the estates of the Church and poor. Sacrilege and proscription are not among the ways and means of our Committee of Supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation of property (especially ecclesiastical property) is condemned as cruel, politically dangerous, and corrosive of trust; protection of property is essential to social order and to prevent degradation and loss of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep Church revenues independent of the Treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: The people of England think that they have constitutional motives, as well as religious, against any project of turning their independent clergy into ecclesiastical pensioners of state. They tremble for their liberty, from the influence of a clergy dependent on the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy should not be made dependent on the central treasury (or be mere crown pensioners) because dependence would compromise ecclesiastical independence and politicize religion; the Church's provision should be stable and protected as property.

rubrics_metrics.name: State provision for religion should be public, visible, and part of high life
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be illuminated with other lights. It will be perfumed with other incense ... with modest splendor, with unassuming state, with mild majesty and sober pomp. ... We will have her to exalt her mitred front in courts and parliaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public rites, buildings, music, and visible religious dignity give people a sense of public worth and social hierarchy that reinforces civic virtue; religious presence should not be relegated to obscurity but integrated into national life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide for religious instruction of all classes, including the poor and the great
rubrics_metrics.description: The Christian statesmen of this land would, indeed, first provide for the multitude ... That the circumstance of the Gospel's being preached to the poor was one of the great tests of its true mission. ... The English people are satisfied, that to the great the consolations of religion are as necessary as its instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious provision and instruction must be universal: the poor require preaching and charity, while the wealthy require instruction and consolation to temper ambition and vice. Public provision fosters social cohesion and moral restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should bind elites to the Church and preserve respect for institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Our education is in a manner wholly in the hands of ecclesiastics ... three fourths of those who go abroad with our young nobility and gentlemen are ecclesiastics: ... By this connection we conceive that we attach our gentlemen to the Church; and we liberalize the Church by an intercourse with the leading characters of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clerical influence in education ties future leaders to established religion, ensuring moral formation and social stability; educational continuity from previous ages preserves patrimony of knowledge while allowing improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware reformers who preach primitive poverty but do not practice it
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall believe those reformers to be then honest enthusiasts, not, as now we think them, cheats and deceivers, when we see them throwing their own goods into common, and submitting their own persons to the austere discipline of the early Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of reformers who advocate returning clergy to primitive poverty without personal sacrifice; such hypocrisy indicates political opportunism rather than genuine moral reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degrading punishments and collective proscription
rubrics_metrics.description: Who but a tyrant ... could think of seizing on the property of men, unaccused, unheard, untried, by whole descriptions, by hundreds and thousands together? ... To drive men from independence to live on alms is itself great cruelty ... this punishment of degradation and infamy is worse than death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass proscription and collective punishment are morally abhorrent and socially destructive; humane and lawful processes must be preserved to prevent degradation that is worse than death.
